svg.desc: Banner for a paper on when response times identify decision and nondecision time in the fixed-parameter diffusion model. Left: two stories for the same experimental condition with an unbiased start, drawn as stacked bars on a seconds axis. Story 1 has distance 0.6 from the start to each boundary, a mean decision time of 0.333 seconds and a fixed nondecision time of 0.250 seconds, total 0.583 seconds. Story 2 halves the boundary distance to 0.3, so its mean decision time is a quarter as long, 0.083 seconds, and adds a random nondecision time with mean 0.500 seconds, again totalling 0.583 seconds. Small glyphs show the two boundary pairs, the second half as far apart. Right: the single exact response-time density that both stories predict, a skewed curve starting at 0.25 seconds with mean 0.583 seconds; the two stories give exactly the same distribution for each response, so no amount of data from this condition can tell them apart. A note says the split becomes determined with a biased start, or with two unbiased conditions that differ in caution or evidence strength. Values are from the paper’s Table 1; boundary distances are in units of square-root seconds with the diffusion coefficient fixed at one.
svg.text: Same data, two stories: how much of a response is deciding?
